To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Treg cell intrinsic NF-κB activity is required for the generation and differentiation of thymic Tregs, but not for their peripheral homeostasis, and pharmacological inhibition of NF-κBs is a potential therapeutic approach to manipulate Treg development.
T cell-intrinsic NF-kappaB signaling is critical for the development of natural regulatory T cells in the thyme.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of regulatory T cells (Treg cells) in the thymic microenvironment, and with the role of NF-κβ in this process.
the molecular mechanisms underlying the differentiation of Treg precursor cells into mature Treg cell.
the development and function of regulatory T cells, a T cell subset critically involved in the maintenance of peripheral tolerance and immune homeostasis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
NF-κB is required for Treg development in the thymic environment, and that NF-κ B is required for the maintenance of Treg cells within the periphery.
NF-κB is a critical regulator of Treg cell development, and that pharmacological inhibition of NF-κ B may represent an interesting therapeutic strategy to modulate Treg cells.

Treg cell development is dependent on TCR-mediated NF-κB-activation, but that this is not sufficient to fully restore the development of Treg cells when TCR-mediated NF-kB-activation is blocked in a cell-intrinsic manner.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the development of Treg cells requires Treg cell-intrisinc NF-κB-activation.
Treg cell development is critically dependent on NF-κB-mediated signaling.
NF-κB is required in the Treg cell lineage to promote the differentiation of Foxp3− Treg precursors into mature Foxp3+ Treg cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the development and homeostasis of natural Treg cells in mice requires TCR/CD28-mediated NF-κB signalling.
NF-κB is required for T cell development and T cell function.
Treg cell differentiation in the thymic cortex is dependent on Treg cell-inherent NF-kappaB activation, which is not compensated for by wild-type cells in the thymi of Tg mice.
